memo.verdict: Neutral; park, with an entry level of about EUR 32 (the modal path clears 20% a year over eighteen months at about EUR 32.4 and over three years at about EUR 29.1). Conviction medium on the business, medium-high on the arithmetic. The park is on return, not on quality: no gate item fires (management C, business quality C, predictability B, trackability B). ABN AMRO is a self-help case riding a contractual rates tailwind, in a mature Dutch deposit bank, bought after the re-rating; compelling as a company change, not compelling as an investment at EUR 40.75. What would un-park it at the current price: a move to semi-annual distributions with a buyback above EUR 1.5bn in February 2027, or a sector de-rating that takes the stock to the entry level on an unchanged path. The record would also re-rate the case rather than wait if Q3 and Q4 2026 print a cost of risk below 8 basis points with NIBC consolidated and costs on the EUR 5.5bn run-rate.
case: The thesis, repeatable. ABN AMRO is a self-help case riding a contractual rates tailwind, in a mature Dutch deposit bank, bought after the re-rating. Compelling as a company change; not compelling as an investment at EUR 40.75, because the price capitalises the fast part of the earnings path at a top-decile multiple and leaves the slow part plus a 4% to 5% dividend yield to pay about 3% a year over eighteen months. It clears the 20% bar only below about EUR 32, or if consensus earnings are delivered and the multiple holds at the top of its ten-year range; neither is the modal case.

The change, internal and external at once, both delivered. A new chief executive (23 April 2025) set the plan at the 25 November 2025 Capital Markets Day: EUR 900m of cost and 5,200 roles out, EUR 10bn of risk-weighted assets out of corporate lending, up to 100% of generated capital returned. 2,340 roles and EUR 300m of savings are done (45% in five quarters); EUR 9bn of corporate risk-weighted assets is out (63%). At the same time the EUR 180bn replicating portfolio began rolling maturing hedges on to swap yields near 3%, lifting the liability margin 5 basis points a quarter; FY2026 commercial net interest income guidance went to about EUR 6.8bn including NIBC from EUR 6.4bn, about EUR 120m above pre-results consensus of EUR 6.68bn, with cost guidance held at about EUR 5.5bn against consensus EUR 5.64bn. CET1 15.9% against 13.75%; the DNB floor expiry on 30 November 2026 releases about EUR 7bn of risk-weighted assets, about 50 basis points of CET1. Internal forces rated A: the screen's rule (chief-executive change plus guidance increase, or three strong forces) is met several times over, and no screen red flag fits (no caretaker chief executive; no PowerPoint transformation; no trivial guidance rise; no crown jewels sold; no empire-building, NIBC bought at 0.85x book; no dangerous leverage; no debt-funded buyback). External forces B: two strong tailwinds (the swap-curve regime; the dated capital release) outweigh two headwinds (Dutch mortgage competition, with asset margins -2 basis points in Q2 2026 and management expecting the compression to persist or accelerate after the floor removal; the Collective Labour Agreement round, unions asking up to 5.5% against a 2% hypothesis at up to EUR 30m a year per 1%). Competition is the one D in 'Change Forces': production share 20% to 18%; Rabobank's savings rate to 1.50% while ABN AMRO and ING held 1.25%; ING's Dutch retail growing deposits and loans more than 7% and Rabobank more than 5%, both faster than ABN AMRO.

'Financial Outputs' have turned up on every reported line (B). Q2 2026 net profit EUR 781m (+29%, 15% above consensus), net interest income +11%, fees +25%, operating income +13% against costs -1.3%, pre-provision profit +36% to EUR 1,123m, cost of risk 4 basis points, return on equity 12.1% (the 2028 target already). The change has travelled the whole 'Six Layer Inputs-outputs' chain: consensus EPS FY2026 to FY2028 +18% to +22% in twelve months; shares +68.5% to EUR 40.75. Key metrics B (near-term "very positive" and continuation plausible: the hedge roll for two to three more years, NIBC's full year, flat costs; then a plateau from 2028). Revenue growth B: from -1.6% (EUR 8,861m to EUR 8,716m) to +13% in Q2 2026 and consensus +10.5% FY2026, +7.4% FY2027, +3.7% FY2028; our modal EUR 9,600m, EUR 10,250m, EUR 10,600m. Margin B: cost-to-income 64.4% all-in in 2025, about 57% implied for 2026, below 55% targeted for 2028, the street at 52% to 53%, our path 52.5%; the retail unit's 60% against ING's 38% keeps it off an A. Net debt equivalent A: 215 basis points of excess capital, EUR 7.5bn or more of distributions against a EUR 33.5bn market capitalisation. Sell-side upgrades C: the near term favours small beats (Q3 on 11 or 13 November; the floor; the February 2027 buyback) but consensus FY2028 revenue EUR 10,734m is 7% above the "above EUR 10bn" target, consensus implies about 52% cost-to-income against "below 55%", consensus implied return on equity 13.7% against "above 12%", and our FY2028 EPS EUR 4.25 is 6% below the consensus median EUR 4.54; upgrades possible, not probable, and from the buyback size and the swap curve rather than the plan. Our FY2026 EPS EUR 3.25 is on guidance and 1% above consensus EUR 3.22 (H1 EUR 1.795; H2 about EUR 0.73 a quarter after the Worldline provision of EUR 31m in Q3, the Alfam loss of EUR 100m in Q4, NIBC integration costs, cost of risk normalising towards 10 basis points). Revision skew B (FactSet mean FY2026 EPS +1.8% one month, +10.2% three, +14.7% six to EUR 3.23; the one-month figure shows the wave fading). Upgrade record B (beat-and-raise since 2024; the 2024 absolute cost target of below EUR 4.7bn missed by EUR 650m under the previous management). Guidance conservatism B (Morgan Stanley called the prior net interest income guidance "highly conservative"; its estimates 5% to 9% ahead of consensus on EPS and 40% ahead on 2027 to 2028 buybacks; the sceptics argue valuation and integration, not guidance). Goldilocks growth B: about 33% FY2026 over FY2025 (above the band, off a depressed base), 14.4% a year FY2026 to FY2028 (EUR 3.25 to EUR 4.25), 12.3% a year FY2026 to FY2029 (EUR 4.60), at the band's floor; beyond 2028, 7% to 8% a year. Staircase B: near steps A (Q3 results; the floor expiry; Alfam closing; February 2027 results with the capital review and the semi-annual question); mid steps B (NIBC synergies; the State's placement; the CFO mandate; EU AML Regulation; replicating yields reaching 3%); far steps C (the 2028 targets; Hauck Aufhäuser Lampe synergies; Worldline; renewed acquisition capacity from H2 2027); none novel.
counter_case: At the whole-case level (the bull case as Morgan Stanley and Jefferies make it, at full force). ABN AMRO is one of the cleanest self-help ideas in European banking and the market has not finished paying for it. The total payout yield is above 10%, sector-leading, with Jefferies counting EUR 8.6bn of distributions over 2026 to 2028 and Morgan Stanley 40% ahead of consensus on 2027 to 2028 buybacks. The 2028 return on tangible equity is 14% to 14.6% on 1.35x 2027 tangible book, with the cost-to-income ratio heading to 52%. Consensus net interest income still rests on guidance that assumes zero replicating-portfolio growth and 100% pass-through on interest-bearing deposits, both of which Q2 2026 disproved (deposits +EUR 5.3bn; pass-through nil), so consensus is still too low, and Morgan Stanley's estimates are 5% to 9% above it on EPS. The State's sell-down from 24.9% to 10.5% turns an overhang into consolidation optionality. A market that pays eleven to twelve times for a bank re-read as a five-year earnings grower (the sector research citing Morgan Stanley) gives about 20% a year over eighteen months on consensus earnings and 9.9x, and more at 11x. The company has beaten every cost and net interest income guide since 2024; the Q2 2026 print itself is the evidence. The record's own arithmetic concedes the point in part: the bull branch gives 19.6% a year over eighteen months and about 15.5% a year over three; at the conceded anchor of 9.9x even our prudent path gives 11.9% and 12.2% a year; and the earnings leg is more secure than most banks' because it is contractual for two to three years. The record also concedes that the cost of risk and other income are the only lines it has cut, that it may be too prudent on costs, and that the multiple's floor is above the five-year history. The record's reply: the bull return needs two conditions at once, consensus earnings that already sit above management's own 2028 targets on income, efficiency and return on equity, and a multiple at or above the ten-year 75th percentile in a sector where two thirds of the 95 banks are already at the 80th percentile or higher and the Banks row lost its Overweight this week; that branch is about 20%; the asymmetry is -25% to -30% at a fair trough with earnings unchanged against about +30% to the bull branch with the modal near zero; and the floor (a 4% to 5% dividend yield; about 1.25x book at a 12% return on equity; Jefferies' bear EUR 30) is the entry level, which is the point of waiting for it.

At the 'Foundations' level (the FALSE FRIEND reading, rated by the risks research the most consistent of its three bear pathways). Temporary strength masks structural retail net interest income decay: Clearing net interest income runs about 50% above run-rate, the cost of risk is a record 4 basis points, risk-weighted-asset optimisation flatters capital, while the short duration of the replicating portfolio (40% to 45% repricing within twelve months) and the NHG mix erode the real margin underneath; the Q2 2026 beat is the peak, not the base, and the 2028 targets are reached on one-offs and then missed on run-rate. The record's reply: the Q2 2026 liability margin rose 5 basis points and commercial net interest income guidance was raised on the hedge roll, not on Clearing; the short duration cuts both ways and the ECB is raising; the cost of risk and other income are conceded as over-earning and normalised in the path, which is one reason our FY2028 EPS sits 6% below consensus. Where it would win: a sequential net interest income fall of more than 2% in Q3 or Q4 2026, or an asset margin down more than 5 basis points in a quarter.
triggers: - Entry: below about EUR 32 (EUR 32.4 on eighteen months; EUR 29.1 on three years), 21% below the 2026-10-12 close.

- Un-park at the current price: semi-annual distributions with a buyback above EUR 1.5bn at the February 2027 results; or a sector de-rating to the entry level on an unchanged path; or Q3 and Q4 2026 printing a cost of risk below 8 basis points with NIBC consolidated and costs on the EUR 5.5bn run-rate.

- Invalidate levels: a sequential net interest income fall of more than 2% in Q3 or Q4 2026; a cost-to-income ratio above 62% for 2026; asset margin down more than 5 basis points in a quarter; the ECB deposit rate priced below 2.0% within eighteen months.

- Alarm levels: commercial net interest income below EUR 6.6bn for FY2026; 2026 costs above EUR 5.6bn; ABN AMRO's savings rate raised above 1.25% in response to Rabobank; cost of risk above 15 basis points for two quarters; two consecutive quarters of net wealth outflows; no buyback announcement with the February 2027 results, or a programme below EUR 1bn; a 24-month-forward multiple above 9.9x with our path unchanged (an alarm on the price, not the case).

- What would change the record's side on each thing the case turns on: the hedge roll (probable, about 70%) fails if the market prices the ECB below 2% within eighteen months or the savings rate goes above 1.25%; costs (probable, about 65%) fail at 2026 costs above EUR 5.6bn or cost-to-income above 62%; capital return (probable, about 70% for at least EUR 1bn and EUR 7.5bn over 2026 to 2028; plausible for EUR 1.5bn) fails with no programme or one below EUR 1bn in February 2027; the multiple holding at or above 9.3x (about 35%) is argued higher by semi-annual distributions and a buyback above EUR 1.5bn, and argued lower by the sector's own-history percentiles falling toward their medians without earnings cuts, which would make the stock cheap on the same path; consensus FY2028 EPS of EUR 4.54 (about 45%) is argued for by Q3 and Q4 2026 printing a cost of risk below 8 basis points with costs on the run-rate.

- The Pret sandwich to watch: a Q3 or Q4 2026 print that misses on costs while the State places stock into a sector de-rating would combine four of six tolerable weaknesses (a 90th-percentile multiple; the post-2028 plateau; the 14% placement; the annual capital review; two integrations at once; a record-low cost of risk).
